title: Agent Frameworks, Harnesses, and Runtimes
objective: Frame the agentic development stack through a practical support-agent workload.
coreClaim: Agentic systems require separable layers for experience, harness, runtime, data, protocols, observability, and release governance.
mechanism: A support operations agent exposes each layer because it needs tools, workflow control, memory, retrieval, approvals, traces, and evals.
example: A support agent looks up accounts, retrieves policy, drafts a reply, pauses for approval, and records outcomes.
practicalTakeaway: Do not evaluate an agent framework without naming the layer it is solving.

title: By the end, the stack should feel separable
objective: Set learning goals for layer separation and workload-fit decisions.
coreClaim: The learner should be able to distinguish model APIs, UI SDKs, harnesses, runtimes, visual builders, observability, evals, and database layers.
mechanism: The deck decomposes one support-agent architecture into stack responsibilities.
example: Tool calling belongs to the harness, checkpointing to the runtime, and eval datasets to the operations layer.
practicalTakeaway: Use precise layer names before comparing products.

title: Support operations agent
objective: Anchor the taxonomy in a realistic workload.
coreClaim: A support operations agent is a useful comparison workload because it combines knowledge, tools, approvals, data, and quality controls.
mechanism: Each required behavior maps to a stack layer.
example: Refund escalation requires retrieval, account lookup, workflow state, approval, audit, and trace evidence.
practicalTakeaway: Compare frameworks against a workload with real operational boundaries.

title: The stack is layered, but products blur layers
coreClaim: Agent products often bundle several layers, but builders still need to reason about each layer independently.
mechanism: One product may provide harness, workflow, storage, tracing, and deployment surfaces.
example: Mastra bundles several TypeScript agent-app concerns; LangChain separates LangChain, LangGraph, and LangSmith surfaces.
practicalTakeaway: Product packaging is not the same as architecture ownership.

title: Use precise names or the stack becomes muddy
coreClaim: Calling everything an agent framework hides important differences between APIs, harnesses, runtimes, builders, databases, and observability platforms.
mechanism: Each category solves a different integration or operational problem.
example: Vercel AI SDK UI solves frontend streaming concerns that LangGraph persistence does not.
practicalTakeaway: Name the problem before naming the tool.

title: Do not start by picking a framework
coreClaim: Framework choice should follow workload shape rather than brand familiarity.
mechanism: Data sensitivity, state lifetime, UI needs, side effects, and release process change the correct stack.
example: A read-only chat UI needs different tooling than a multi-step refund workflow.
practicalTakeaway: Start with promises the product makes to users and operators.

title: Model and provider APIs are the substrate
objective: Separate provider APIs from agent frameworks.
coreClaim: Provider APIs supply model calls, tool-call formats, structured outputs, and streaming primitives, but do not by themselves define a full product runtime.
mechanism: Frameworks build harness and runtime behavior on top of provider capabilities.
example: OpenAI Agents SDK adds agent primitives on top of model execution and tracing concepts.
practicalTakeaway: Treat provider features as substrate, not the entire architecture.

title: UI and application integration can be its own layer
coreClaim: Frontend streaming, tool rendering, and generative UI are real integration problems separate from durable workflow runtime.
mechanism: UI SDKs manage message streams, tool results, component rendering, and client/server transport.
example: Vercel AI SDK UI supports generative interfaces that render tool-driven UI states.
practicalTakeaway: Do not force a workflow runtime to solve frontend experience problems.

title: Provider-native agent runtime with few primitives
coreClaim: Provider-native agent SDKs can be useful when teams want a compact agent loop with built-in primitives such as handoffs, guardrails, and tracing.
mechanism: The SDK packages common agent concerns around provider model execution.
example: OpenAI Agents SDK exposes agent, handoff, guardrail, and tracing concepts.
practicalTakeaway: Use provider-native runtimes when close provider alignment matters more than broad ecosystem layering.

title: The harness is where "agent" becomes product behavior
coreClaim: The harness wraps the model loop with tools, prompts, context, middleware, and invocation behavior.
mechanism: LangChain describes the harness as the context/tooling around the model-tool loop.
example: Middleware can add retries, guardrails, summarization, or human approval around model/tool calls.
practicalTakeaway: Use harnesses to shape model behavior into product behavior.

title: Tools are the hard boundary between language and action
coreClaim: Tools are the boundary where model intent becomes validated application action.
mechanism: Tool descriptions and schemas guide model selection and validate arguments before execution.
example: Vercel AI SDK tools define descriptions, input schemas, optional execution, and approval behavior.
practicalTakeaway: Keep permissions and validation at tool boundaries, not in prompt text alone.

title: LangChain is the broad harness and integration ecosystem
coreClaim: LangChain's agent value is broad harness configurability and integration depth.
mechanism: LangChain agents combine model, tools, prompt, structured output, middleware, context, and checkpointer support.
example: A support agent can use LangChain tools and middleware while relying on LangGraph-backed persistence.
practicalTakeaway: Choose LangChain when broad integrations and harness flexibility matter.

title: Mastra packages the TypeScript agent stack as one product shape
coreClaim: Mastra focuses on a TypeScript product-stack approach to agents, workflows, memory, and observability.
mechanism: Mastra agent and workflow docs expose TypeScript-centered primitives for agent applications.
example: A Node or Next.js team can keep agent code in the same TypeScript project shape.
practicalTakeaway: Choose Mastra when TypeScript stack coherence reduces delivery friction.

title: ADK is an agent app framework with workflow agents and runtime services
coreClaim: Google ADK provides agent app framework concepts plus workflow-agent and runtime-service concepts.
mechanism: ADK docs distinguish agents, runtime, graph workflows, multi-agent workflows, sessions, memory, and observability.
example: Workflow agents can manage execution flow among sub-agents, while graph workflows provide more flexible control.
practicalTakeaway: Consider ADK when Google ecosystem/runtime alignment matters.

title: Microsoft's stack makes agents and workflows first-class
coreClaim: Microsoft Agent Framework treats agents and workflows as first-class developer concepts inside Microsoft's ecosystem.
mechanism: The Microsoft overview frames agent and workflow development as coordinated framework capabilities.
example: Teams already standardized on Microsoft developer tooling may prefer this integration surface.
practicalTakeaway: Evaluate Microsoft Agent Framework through ecosystem fit and workflow needs.

title: LlamaIndex starts from the data problem
coreClaim: LlamaIndex is most naturally positioned around data, indexing, retrieval, and agent workflows over knowledge sources.
mechanism: Its docs organize agent building alongside RAG, indexing, querying, and workflow guidance.
example: A knowledge-heavy support agent may use LlamaIndex patterns for data loading and querying.
practicalTakeaway: Choose LlamaIndex when the hardest problem is data-to-context.

title: Agno leans into the agent platform/control-plane problem
coreClaim: Agno emphasizes building and running an agent platform, including runtime, sessions, tracing, RBAC, audit logs, and a control plane.
mechanism: Agno docs describe SDK, AgentOS runtime, APIs, storage, observability, security, and scheduling.
example: A team building a fleet of in-product agents may value AgentOS-style platform management.
practicalTakeaway: Choose platform-oriented tooling when the problem is operating many agents, not one demo agent.

title: Runtimes exist because real work outlives one model call
coreClaim: Long-running work requires state, retries, branches, persistence, and resume behavior beyond one model call.
mechanism: Runtimes provide execution boundaries where state can be persisted and inspected.
example: A support workflow may classify, retrieve, draft, pause for approval, then execute later.
practicalTakeaway: Use a runtime when the work must survive time, failure, or review.

title: LangGraph is the stateful runtime under many LangChain agents
coreClaim: LangGraph provides stateful graph runtime capabilities such as persistence, interrupts, memory, and event streaming.
mechanism: Graphs model state and control flow so execution can be inspected, resumed, and governed.
example: A LangChain agent can rely on graph persistence for conversation history and checkpointing.
practicalTakeaway: Reach for LangGraph when control flow and durable state become product logic.

title: Mastra uses workflows for explicit TypeScript processes
coreClaim: Mastra workflows make TypeScript business processes explicit when agent improvisation is not enough.
mechanism: Workflow APIs model ordered steps and control flow inside the Mastra stack.
example: A ticket escalation process can be modeled as workflow steps with approval boundaries.
practicalTakeaway: Promote high-risk or auditable behavior into explicit workflow code.

title: Google and Microsoft also draw the agent/workflow boundary
objective: Show that workflow separation is ecosystem-wide.
coreClaim: Major ecosystems increasingly distinguish open-ended agents from explicit workflows.
mechanism: ADK workflow-agent and graph-workflow docs, plus Microsoft Agent Framework overview, show this boundary.
example: ADK workflow agents manage execution flow among sub-agents.
practicalTakeaway: Expect workflow boundaries to appear across mature agent stacks.

title: Low-code builders are orchestration products, not toys
coreClaim: Low-code AI builders can represent serious orchestration, integration, and operations work.
mechanism: n8n, Langflow, and Flowise expose triggers, agents, tools, workflow state, checkpoints, and visual composition.
example: Flowise Agentflow V2 documents explicit workflow paths, state, checkpoints, HITL, and MCP tools.
practicalTakeaway: Evaluate low-code tools by integration and control needs, not by stigma.

title: n8n is strongest at evented operations glue
coreClaim: n8n is strongest when the workload is evented automation across existing SaaS, APIs, and operational systems.
mechanism: n8n AI workflow and AI Agent node docs show agents embedded in broader automation flows.
example: A support escalation can trigger from a ticket event, call an AI agent node, update CRM, and notify Slack.
practicalTakeaway: Use n8n when integration glue is the dominant workload.

title: Visual builders make composition legible
coreClaim: Visual builders make tool wiring, model provider selection, flow state, and handoffs easier to inspect.
mechanism: Langflow and Flowise expose agent components, tools, flow state, and workflow connections visually.
example: Langflow Tool Mode turns components into tools for an Agent component.
practicalTakeaway: Use visual builders when composition legibility beats code-level abstraction.

title: The question is not low-code versus code
coreClaim: The useful question is where each piece of logic should live for ownership, auditability, reuse, and iteration speed.
mechanism: Some logic belongs in code, some in workflows, and some in operator-managed integration maps.
example: Authorization belongs in code; a notification routing workflow may belong in n8n.
practicalTakeaway: Put logic where it can be owned and tested responsibly.

title: Databases are the agent's product memory, not just vector search
coreClaim: Agent databases must support operational truth, semantic retrieval, memory, checkpoints, audit, and eval data.
mechanism: RAG, memory, checkpoints, and product data have different schemas, guarantees, and retention policies.
example: An order record, retrieved policy chunk, checkpoint snapshot, and eval dataset should not be treated as one vague memory bucket.
practicalTakeaway: Name database responsibilities before picking a storage product.

title: MongoDB fits when operational data and semantic search should sit together
coreClaim: MongoDB is compelling when document operational data and semantic/vector search should live close together.
mechanism: MongoDB Vector Search and LangChain integrations support vector stores, retrievers, and hybrid search patterns over MongoDB data.
example: A support agent can retrieve policy and operational account context from MongoDB-backed collections.
practicalTakeaway: Use MongoDB where flexible operational records and retrieval context are tightly coupled.

title: Postgres fits when relational integrity and vectors should share a transaction boundary
coreClaim: Postgres with pgvector is compelling when relational integrity and vector similarity search need to share database boundaries.
mechanism: pgvector adds vector similarity search capabilities to Postgres.
example: A billing workflow may want relational constraints and embedding records inside one transactional database environment.
practicalTakeaway: Use Postgres/pgvector when relational consistency is the primary database concern.

title: RAG is a data product pipeline, not a one-line tool
coreClaim: RAG requires document processing, chunking, embedding, vector storage, retrieval, evaluation, and freshness policies.
mechanism: Mastra RAG docs describe chunking, embeddings, vector storage, and retrieval as explicit steps.
example: A policy corpus must be chunked, embedded, stored, queried, and evaluated before it reliably supports support answers.
practicalTakeaway: Treat RAG as a maintained data product.

title: Memory means several different things
coreClaim: Memory can mean message history, working memory, semantic recall, observational summaries, or durable product records.
mechanism: Mastra memory docs separate message history, working memory, semantic recall, and observational memory.
example: Remembering a user's preferred language is different from retrieving an old support conversation by semantic similarity.
practicalTakeaway: Specify memory type, scope, retention, and correction path.

title: Checkpoints are different from memories
coreClaim: Checkpoints preserve execution state, while memories represent context the product chooses to carry forward.
mechanism: LangGraph persistence stores state and execution progress for thread-based resume and inspection.
example: A paused approval workflow checkpoint is not a user preference memory.
practicalTakeaway: Do not use memory stores as workflow recovery systems.

title: Observability turns agent behavior into inspectable evidence
coreClaim: Agent observability captures the evidence needed to debug model, tool, retrieval, workflow, and memory behavior.
mechanism: LangSmith and Langfuse expose tracing and observability concepts for LLM applications.
example: A trace can show which policy chunk, tool output, and model call led to a bad support response.
practicalTakeaway: Instrument decisions and dependencies, not only exceptions.

title: LangSmith is the LangChain ecosystem control plane
coreClaim: LangSmith provides observability and evaluation depth for LangChain/LangGraph workflows.
mechanism: LangSmith docs cover traces, debugging, evaluation, datasets, and experiments.
example: A LangGraph support workflow can use LangSmith traces and evals to diagnose regressions.
practicalTakeaway: Use LangSmith when the LangChain ecosystem is central to the workflow.

title: Langfuse is framework-independent LLM observability and evals
coreClaim: Langfuse focuses on framework-independent LLM tracing, observability, datasets, experiments, and evaluation.
mechanism: Langfuse docs frame evals as repeatable checks that catch regressions before shipping.
example: A Mastra or custom agent can send traces and use Langfuse evals outside the LangChain stack.
practicalTakeaway: Use framework-independent observability when the stack is mixed.

title: A production agent team needs a release process
objective: Connect traces and evals to delivery.
coreClaim: Production agents need a release loop around traces, datasets, experiments, scores, and gates.
mechanism: Observability finds cases; datasets preserve them; evals compare changes; release gates prevent regressions.
example: A failed refund response becomes a regression case before the next prompt or model change ships.
practicalTakeaway: Treat agent behavior changes like software releases.

title: Protocols reduce glue, but do not erase ownership
coreClaim: MCP and A2A reduce custom integration glue, but teams still own auth, data policy, quality, and workflow semantics.
mechanism: MCP standardizes context/tool access patterns; A2A standardizes agent-to-agent task communication patterns.
example: A tool can be exposed over MCP, but the owning service still controls authorization and audit.
practicalTakeaway: Use protocols as boundaries, not governance substitutes.

title: Human approval is a runtime feature, not a prompt
coreClaim: Human approval requires pause, persistence, resume, audit, and UI state, so it belongs in runtime design.
mechanism: Tool approval and workflow/HITL docs show approval as an execution state, not just a prompt instruction.
example: A payment tool approval needs a saved request, decision record, and resumed execution.
practicalTakeaway: Put approval before side effects and make it durable.

title: Pick by workload shape
coreClaim: The right tool depends on UI needs, data needs, runtime needs, stack language, integration shape, governance, and release discipline.
mechanism: Each product category optimizes a different part of the stack.
example: A TypeScript UI-heavy app may choose Vercel AI SDK plus Mastra; a stateful graph workflow may choose LangGraph.
practicalTakeaway: Make the selected stack match the hard part of the workload.

title: A realistic support agent architecture
coreClaim: A realistic support agent architecture includes experience, harness, runtime, data plane, protocols, operations, and governance layers.
mechanism: Each layer owns one class of runtime or product risk.
example: The architecture includes chat UI, agent harness, workflow runtime, MongoDB/Postgres, MCP/A2A, traces, evals, and audit.
practicalTakeaway: Build the architecture from responsibilities, then map products.

title: What tooling is really buying you
coreClaim: Tooling buys standard contracts, inspectable state, integration speed, durable execution, traceability, and regression control.
mechanism: Frameworks and platforms reduce custom glue where their abstraction matches the workload.
example: LangGraph buys stateful execution; Langfuse buys framework-independent traces and evals; n8n buys integration workflow speed.
practicalTakeaway: Adopt tooling where it removes a real operational burden.

title: The stack fits together when each layer owns one job
coreClaim: The stack becomes maintainable when each layer has a clear job and handoff boundary.
mechanism: Clear layer ownership prevents prompts, tools, databases, workflows, and evals from becoming tangled.
example: Tool schema owns action shape; runtime owns execution state; database owns durable truth; evals own release evidence.
practicalTakeaway: Keep ownership boundaries explicit as the agent matures.

title: Sources used to build this deck
coreClaim: The references are grouped by framework category so learners can follow the stack layer they care about.
mechanism: Each reference group maps to a major deck concept: frameworks, UI/builders, protocols, data/memory, or observability/evals.
example: Read LangGraph docs for runtime state and Langfuse docs for framework-independent evals.
practicalTakeaway: Use current primary docs for API details because the ecosystem moves quickly.
